prompt: Explain why we only ever see one side of the Moon from Earth, and correct the common misconception that the Moon doesn't rotate at all.
reference_answer: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth -- it does rotate, but once per orbit, so the same face always points toward Earth; it is not stationary/non-rotating.
notes: tests correction of a specific, commonly-held wrong belief
model_response: The reason we only see one side of the Moon from Earth is because it takes the Moon about 27.3 days to complete one orbit around our planet, which is roughly the same amount of time it takes for it to rotate once on its axis. This means that the same face of the Moon is always pointing towards us as it orbits the Earth, making it appear as though we're only seeing one side. The Moon does indeed rotate, but its rotation period matches its orbital period around the Earth, resulting in this unique phenomenon known as tidal locking.
judge_reasoning: The model accurately explains that the Moon is tidally locked to Earth, rotates once per orbit, and explicitly corrects the misconception that the Moon does not rotate at all.

CORRECTNESS: CORRECT  
BEHAVIOR: MET
